content: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a spiral-shaped bacterium that resides in the gastric mucosa. Its global prevalence exceeds 50%, with higher rates observed in developing countries and among older populations. The infection is typically acquired during childhood through oral transmission and often persists throughout life without causing symptoms. Currently, there is no effective vaccine available to prevent H. pylori infection. The only treatment option involves the use of antimicrobial agents, either alone or in combination with acid-suppressive drugs, to eradicate the bacterium from the gastric mucosa. In a minority of infected individuals, H. pylori can lead to severe complications, including gastric ulcers, duodenal ulcers, and gastric carcinoma. For symptomatic individuals, eradication of the infection is recommended to prevent these complications. The standard treatment for H. pylori eradication is triple therapy, which consists of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), clarithromycin, and either amoxicillin or metronidazole, administered for 10 to 14 days. However, this regimen achieves eradication in only about 70% of treated patients. This suboptimal success rate is attributed to factors such as poor patient compliance, host-specific factors, bacterial strain variations, and resistance to clarithromycin and metronidazole. Compliance is often hindered by adverse effects of the therapy, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a metallic taste, which can make the treatment intolerable for some patients. The low eradication rate of H. pylori is concerning, as successful eradication has been shown to provide significant clinical benefits. These include the resolution of dyspepsia symptoms, healing of gastro-duodenal ulcers, and a reduced risk of developing gastric carcinoma. Therefore, it is essential to optimize the efficacy of antibacterial therapy against H. pylori. Two main strategies have been explored to improve eradication rates: (1) enhancing antibacterial regimens, such as using triple therapy with quinolones or macrolides, quadruple therapy, or sequential therapy, and (2) improving patient compliance by minimizing adverse effects. Probiotics have been investigated as an adjunct to various antibacterial regimens for H. pylori eradication. Several studies suggest that probiotic supplementation during anti-H. pylori therapy may enhance eradication rates. Probiotics are thought to work through several mechanisms. They improve drug tolerance, thereby increasing therapy completion rates. They also reduce the antibiotic-associated side effects of anti-H. pylori therapy. Additionally, probiotics exhibit immunomodulatory effects by balancing the local production of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines. Furthermore, probiotics are believed to exert direct bacteriostatic and bactericidal effects against infectious agents. Despite these promising findings, the evidence regarding the efficacy of probiotic supplementation in improving H. pylori eradication rates remains inconsistent. Studies have reported varying results, which may be due to differences in the type of probiotics used (bacterial or fungal species), their dosage and duration, the type of antibiotics employed (e.g., amoxicillin, clarithromycin, metronidazole), and the duration of antibiotic therapy (7, 10, or 14 days). These variations make it challenging to draw definitive conclusions about the role of probiotics in H. pylori eradication. Therefore, a systematic review of the available evidence is necessary to clarify the potential benefits of probiotic supplementation in this context.
